new_statements.quote: Luwo has three distinctive tonemes, namely high, mid, and low, which may be combined as rising and falling tone sequences. Besides having lexical functions, tone also has grammatical functions, which include the formation of verbal stems, e.g.: [...] Stress is also clearly audible in Luwo, but as this phenomenon has not yet been studied in any detail in this language, no generalisation can be made.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (TUFS repository record 7676,; image-only, encrypted copy:no, hence the scanned), re-rendered p. 3 at 130 dpi and read the page image myself. The quoted passage is verbatim on p. 3: the tone paragraph "Luwo has three distinctive tonemes, namely high, mid, and low, which may be combined as rising and falling tone sequences. Besides having lexical functions, tone also has grammatical functions, which include the formation of verbal stems, e.g.:" followed by examples (5.a) transitive stems and (5.b) aspect stems, then the last paragraph of sec. 2 Phonology: "Stress is also clearly audible in Luwo, but as this phenomenon has not yet been studied in any detail in this language, no general…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Luwo is a three-tone language (H, M, L, with rising and falling sequences; tone is both lexical and grammatical). The author states that stress is clearly audible but has not been studied, so no rule for its placement is given. Ancillary facts from the same source: roots are always monosyllabic (sec. 3.1.1, p. 4) and affixes are mostly single (C)V suffixes, so any word-level stress would necessarily be near the root.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the source explicitly declines to generalise.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level phonology sketch based on elicited data from Luwo speakers in Khartoum (2000-2007); the statement is about the language in general, not citation forms specifically. Gilley 2004 (OPSL 9, p. 169) independently confirms three level tones for Luwo and says nothing about stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Statement concerns Luwo proper (Jur/Dhe Luwo, ISO lwo, luwo1239) as spoken by consultants in Khartoum from the Wau area; Storch 2010 p. 1 says northern/southern dialect variation is negligible. Thuri (Glottolog: sister language under the Luwo-Thuri node luwo1240) is said to use Luwo materials but is not described here.

sources.note: No sentence on stress, accent or tone. Para. 5 summarises ch. 2 (pp. 19-34): consonant and vowel phonemes, breathy vs non-breathy and long vs short vowels, mostly monosyllabic morphemes, vowel harmony, syllable constraints.

sources.citation: Gilley, Leoma G. 2004. The Lwoian family. Occasional Papers in the Study of Sudanese Languages 9: 165-174. Entebbe: SIL-Sudan.
sources.note: Comparative orthography overview. Sec. 4 Tone p. 169: 'All the Lwoian languages included here have three level tones and at least some have contour tones on short vowels... Luwo writes tone on specific words where meaning would otherwise be unclear.' No statement on Luwo stress; the stress remarks (pp. 171-172) concern Shilluk suffixes only.
